To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mutant Ras isoform-specific downstream signaling is growth factor and cell context dependent and occurs at the level of Raf activation.

the isoform-specific Ras signaling in SW48 cells is growth factor dependent and highly context dependent, and that the requirement for growth factor stimulation occurs early in the Raf activation process.

Ras isoform signaling specificity is highly growth factor dependent and that Ras signaling does not follow the dogma of Ras isoform-specific effector activation derived from ectopic overexpression studies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isoform specificity and context dependence of mutant Ras signaling in human cancer cells.
the role of Ras isoform specificity in the activation of Ras effectors in response to growth factor signaling and oncogenic Ras activation.
the role of growth factors and their receptors in regulating Ras isoform-specific downstream signaling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mutant Ras isoforms are not sufficient to induce signaling in the absence of a growth factor input.
mutant Ras signaling in the absence of mitogens is minimal, and the requirement of growth factor stimulation for mutant Ras signaling is highly context dependent.
mutant Ras isoforms are not biologically interchangeable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mutant KRAS signaling is highly growth factor-dependent and that isoform specificity is highly context-dependent.
Ras isoform specificity is highly context dependent and is not simply dictated by the relative expression levels of Ras isoforms in a given cell type.
the Ras isoform-specificity of Ras effector activation is highly dependent on growth factor inputs, and that this phenomenon is context dependent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ras isoforms are not interchangeable in vivo and that their signaling outputs are highly dependent on the cellular context.
Ras isoform specificity in cancer cells is a function of growth factor signaling and that Ras isoforms are not biologically interchangeable in the absence of mitogenic stimuli.
Ras isoform specificity is highly sensitive to growth factor inputs.
